term: Hubert Dreyfus's views on artificial intelligence
definition: Hubert Dreyfus was a critic of artificial intelligence research.
details: In a series of papers and books, including Alchemy and AI (1965), What Computers Can't Do (1972; 1979; 1992) and Mind over Machine (1986), he presented a skeptical and cautious assessment of AI's progress and a critique of the philosophical foundations of the field. Dreyfus' objections are discussed in most introductions to the philosophy of artificial intelligence, including Russell & Norvig (2021), a standard AI textbook, and in Fearn (2007), a survey of contemporary philosophy. Dreyfus argued that human intelligence and expertise depend primarily on yet-to-be understood informal and unconscious processes rather than symbolic manipulation and that these essentially human skills cannot be fully captured in formal rules. His critique was based on the insights of modern continental philosophers such as Merleau-Ponty and Heidegger, and was directed at the first wave of AI research which tried to reduce intelligence to high level formal symbols. When Dreyfus' ideas were first introduced in the mid-1960s, they were met in the AI community with ridicule and outright hostility. explainer.lead: Hubert Dreyfus was a prominent critic of artificial intelligence research, arguing in a series of papers and books that the field's philosophical foundations were shaky. His objections are discussed in most introductions to the philosophy of AI, including Russell & Norvig, making them a standard reference point in the field.

tiers.eli5: He was a thinker who kept asking whether the people building thinking machines had really understood what thinking is, and he wrote down his doubts in well-known books.
tiers.practitioner: AI researchers encounter Dreyfus's arguments when justifying or critiquing symbolic, rule-based approaches. A pitfall is dismissing his critique as outdated without engaging the specific philosophical objections.
tiers.paperLevel: The given facts state only that Dreyfus presented a skeptical, cautious assessment of AI progress and a critique of the field's philosophical foundations across Alchemy and AI (1965), What Computers Can't Do (1972; 1979; 1992) and Mind over Machine (1986).

explainer.example: A textbook chapter on the philosophy of AI would cite Dreyfus's What Computers Can't Do as the classic statement of skepticism about AI's progress.
